conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you during this admission. You’re here for abdominal pain and vomiting again, correct?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s the same pain I’ve had before—right in the upper belly, going to my back. And I’ve been vomiting, sometimes with a little blood.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you were just discharged three days ago for something similar. Did the prednisone help at all?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It made me feel worse, actually. More nauseous. I couldn’t keep anything down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. We’re going to hold the prednisone this time since it seemed to make your nausea worse instead of helping the pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s fine. But I’m worried—why does this keep happening?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your chronic pancreatitis, likely from your vasculitis, is flaring again. We’re treating it with IV fluids and pain meds for now. We also did a CT scan earlier—no blockage or complications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember the last time I had a scan. Was it the same kind?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Actually, we did an X-ray of your abdomen today. It showed no obstruction, which is good. Just some stool buildup, but nothing urgent.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. And my pain meds—are they helping?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re using IV Dilaudid, which is stronger than what you take by mouth. It should help more, especially since you can’t keep pills down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m also on pantoprazole for my stomach. Should I keep taking that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but since you’re not eating right now, we’ve switched you to IV famotidine. It’s similar but safer for IV use, especially since you’re allergic to IV PPIs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh right, I forgot about that allergy. So what’s the plan now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep you NPO—nothing by mouth—for now to let your pancreas rest. We’ll give fluids and meds through your IV. Once the pain settles, we’ll try small sips and advance your diet slowly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my other meds—like methotrexate and Plaquenil?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll keep your methotrexate—it helps control your vasculitis. We’re restarting Plaquenil too, since it’s important for your Sjogren’s and immune system.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ve been missing doses because I feel so bad during flares.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. That’s why we need to work with your rheumatologist to find a better long-term plan to prevent these frequent admissions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. You’re looking better today. Pain improving?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, much better. I haven’t needed pain meds as often.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. Your labs came back—lipase is normal, which means your pancreas isn’t actively inflamed. We’re going to try clear liquids today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I have water or broth?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, exactly. Start slow. If you keep that down, we’ll move to soft foods tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my stomach—could the pain also be from gastritis?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. That’s why we’re continuing the famotidine. Once you can take pills, we’ll switch back to Protonix, which you were on before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’ve also been feeling lightheaded when I stand. Is that still from my POTS?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your tachycardia is still being managed with betaxolol and fludrocortisone. We’re monitoring it, and you should keep taking those meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. One more thing—my urine test came back abnormal, didn’t it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, there was a bacterial growth, but it’s likely contamination. However, we’re giving you a short course of Macrobid just in case it’s a mild UTI.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. Is that safe with my kidneys?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your kidney function is normal. We checked your creatinine—it’s 0.5, which is excellent.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’ve done really well. You’re tolerating food, pain is controlled, and you’re ready for discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What meds will I go home with?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue betaxolol, fludrocortisone, methotrexate, folic acid, escitalopram, and now Plaquenil. For stomach protection, you’ll take Protonix twice daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And for pain if it comes back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll get hydromorphone suppositories—3 mg every four hours as needed. Use them if you can’t keep pills down. Also, Zofran for nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the Macrobid?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, take it twice a day for four days. It’s just a precaution for the possible UTI.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You have an appointment with Dr. ___ in a few days. It’s very important to go and discuss better control of your vasculitis to prevent future flares.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll make sure to go. I don’t want to keep coming back like this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll help you with that. In the meantime, call your doctor or come back if you develop fever, worsening pain, or can’t keep fluids down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thank you for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’re also giving you parenteral nutrition today before discharge, just to support you at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that the IV nutrition?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, a concentrated infusion to help with your malabsorption. It’ll be given once before you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. I’ve been losing weight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We want to support your nutrition while we work on long-term solutions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate that. I feel much better already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Glad to hear it. We’ll get the discharge papers ready. You should be home within a few hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Dr. Lee.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The nutrition team is starting your parenteral infusion now. This will help support your calorie and nutrient intake at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I see the IV bag. How long will this take?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: About two hours. Then you’ll be all set to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your infusion is complete. I’ve reviewed your discharge instructions again with the nurse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. I feel ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Remember—follow up, take your meds, and come back if anything worsens.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again for everything.
